content: 1. Many studies did not require all participants to undergo bacteriological testing. Instead, tuberculosis (TB) negative classification was often based on chest X-ray (CXR) results and symptoms, introducing incorporation bias. 2. Approximately one-third of the studies were at high risk of bias due to issues with participant flow and timing. 3. Among participants who required bacteriological testing according to the study protocol, fewer than 95% had results available. 4. There was a very wide range in point estimates for sensitivity (18% to 100%), with overlapping confidence intervals (CIs). Some of the heterogeneity could be attributed to economic regions. 5. The confidence intervals around false negatives were relatively narrow compared to the point estimates. 6. Due to the low prevalence of TB in the studies, issues with the reference standard and participant flow/timing had a greater impact on sensitivity than specificity. 7. Point estimates for specificity ranged widely (13% to 99%) without overlapping CIs. No statistically significant variables were identified to explain this heterogeneity. 8. The confidence intervals around false positives were such that the proportion of the population requiring follow-up testing could vary by nearly a factor of two, which has significant resource implications. 9. The general population category in the studies included diverse groups such as adults in prisons, household contacts of TB patients, and miners. This raises concerns about the applicability of findings to the broader population. 10. One study included a small number of children under 15 years old, deviating from the intended study population. This led to a two-level downgrade for indirectness. 11. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 33% to 100%, with variability partly explained by the inclusion of different high-risk groups. This resulted in a one-level downgrade for inconsistency. 12. The 95% credible intervals (CrIs) were wide, and decisions could vary depending on which limits were assumed. However, no further downgrade was applied for imprecision, as inconsistency had already been accounted for. 13. The desirable effects of TB screening include correctly identifying individuals with active TB (true positives) for timely diagnosis and treatment, as well as correctly ruling out TB in those without the disease (true negatives), avoiding unnecessary diagnostic evaluations and enabling alternative diagnoses or preventive therapy. 14. The scale and balance of desirable and undesirable effects vary depending on epidemiological conditions and the intensity of the screening intervention. 15. For screening tests such as symptoms, CXR, and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs), the desirable effects depend heavily on the diagnostic test used after screening. 16. Data presented only relate to one round of screening, and the long-term effects of repeated screening rounds are not captured. 17. Undesirable effects of TB screening include false positives, which can lead to anxiety, unnecessary diagnostic evaluations, and inappropriate treatment with associated social, economic, and health consequences. 18. False negatives result in missed opportunities for treatment, delayed care, continued transmission, and potentially inappropriate preventive therapy, increasing the risk of drug resistance. 19. False-positive screening results could be mitigated by subsequent diagnostic steps in the screening algorithm. However, over-treatment of latent TB infection may still occur, which could reduce the TB burden in the long term. 20. The certainty of evidence for test accuracy varies. For CXR (suggestive of TB), the certainty is low. For prolonged cough, any cough, any TB symptoms, CXR (any abnormality), and mWRDs, the certainty is very low. 21. The direct benefits and adverse effects of screening tests are unknown. Potential adverse effects include anxiety and time burden for patients, while potential benefits include the detection of other conditions. 22. The radiation dose from CXR is low, corresponding to 1/30 of the average annual environmental radiation dose. Innovations in X-ray technology have further reduced radiation exposure. However, children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to ionizing radiation. 23. Infection control is a concern when conducting mWRD tests, as sputum production may generate aerosols, potentially transmitting TB or other respiratory pathogens. Infection control measures must be followed when using mWRDs with sputum samples. 24. The primary goal of active TB screening is early detection and prompt treatment to reduce poor treatment outcomes, health sequelae, and adverse social and economic consequences, as well as to help reduce TB transmission. 25. Children under 5 years old who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases and do not have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment (strong recommendation, high certainty). 26. Adults and adolescents who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases and do not have active TB may be given TB preventive treatment (conditional recommendation, low certainty). 27. People living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care (strong recommendation, high certainty). 28. Treatment of drug-sensitive TB is highly effective (~90%), while treatment of multidrug-resistant TB can also be effective (~70%). Preventive therapy effectiveness ranges from 60% to 90%.
